extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students of literary craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling point of view and on dramatizing inner life in novels — showing a character's consciousness through surface impressions, scenes and dialogue rather than by retrospective exposition. Uses Henry James's practice (The Ambassadors, The Wings of the Dove) as primary examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the story from the character whose vision effects the change
rubrics_metrics.description: The story must be told from Strether’s point of view because the change in his purpose is due to a change in his vision; the reader must share his vision to follow the long slow process of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a central consciousness when the subject is fundamentally an impression or a mind's transformation; if the change is internal, narration should be limited to the field of that character's vision. Example: The Ambassadors must be seen from Strether’s viewpoint because outward behaviour alone would not express his inner revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame all description as impressions filtered through the chosen consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject consists entirely of an impression received by a certain man; nothing that any one else could discern would give the full sense of the eventful life within.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render setting, other characters, and atmosphere as they strike upon the protagonist's senses — e.g., Paris and spring-time are Strether's picture. Do not stray beyond that field of vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from authorial intrusions and authoritative explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The author most carefully refrains from using his knowledge; he wishes us to accept nothing from him, on authority—only to watch and learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid telling the reader 'what it all means' or supplying extraneous facts from the author's omniscience. Let the reader infer from presented images and scenes rather than from authorial summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize inner thought by showing its surface manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: We must see Strether’s thought made intelligible by a direct view of its surface: the immediate flaw or ripple of the moment, and the next, will take up the tale like speakers in a dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of exposition of thought, present the passing images, gestures, sensory flashes, small hesitations and scenes that reveal the operation of the mind. Treat mental life as enacted drama rather than summarized report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retrospective tabulation of reasons — show the change by moments
rubrics_metrics.description: To announce the fact, with a tabulation of his reasons, would be the historic, retrospective, undramatic way; multiply glimpses at different moments when the mind is brushed by new experience so the silent change is apparent without explicit statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sequence of small scenes and impressions across time to make a character's change visible; do not compress into a single explanatory speech or summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make the protagonist the full autobiographical narrator when suspense or partial knowledge is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the book were cast autobiographically and Strether spoke in person he could not hold back; he would have to tell all, and his narration would discount the effect of sudden dramatic moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a narrator admitting us to his mind would destroy suspense or surprise (e.g., a murderer cannot reliably narrate a mystery), withhold full first-person confession and instead dramatize the mind externally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenic dialogue to supply necessary backstory instead of lumps of narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversation between Strether and Maria Gostrey puts the reader in possession of all the past facts necessary; a scene takes the place of that 'harking back to make up' lump of narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work exposition into scenes and dialogue so the reader learns context through enacted interaction rather than through narrative dumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow the narrative method to secure dramatic effects even when subject is undramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the subject may be non-dramatic (a pictorial or descriptive subject), the author can secure all the effects of true drama by dramatizing the picture of somebody’s experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply dramatic techniques — staging, timing, restraint, sudden speech — to descriptive material to give it force and authority (e.g., Strether’s brooding chapters become dramatic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the authorial role unobtrusive — vanish like a playwright
rubrics_metrics.description: The author’s part in the narration is unobtrusive to the last degree; his role is no more than that of a playwright who vanishes and leaves his people to act the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize explicit commentary, judgment, or explanation from the authorial voice; orchestrate scenes so the characters and images enact the story on their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat scenes as dramatic while remaining within protagonist’s vision
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene is kept framed in Strether’s vision but the author keeps his consciousness out of sight; the scene is treated as dramatically as possible while remaining within the character's field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may present scenes with objective dramatic relief even though everything is filtered through POV; the reader can feel 'outside' the character briefly while still receiving content through that character's senses — done carefully to avoid breaking method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surround a hidden fact and let it emerge by implication rather than stating it
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to walk straight up to the fact and put it into phrases, but to surround the fact, and so to detach it inviolate — Henry James's manner of dramatizing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use implication: give partial glimpses, suggestive details, small revealing moments so that the reader 'becomes possessed' of the fact later, often noticing the exact word that made it clear only on re-reading (example: Milly’s secret disease and feelings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply peripheral glimpses to give three-dimensional solidity to a mind
rubrics_metrics.description: By showing the outer rim of a person's consciousness from different angles (a little look, a pause, an unexplained motion), the author enables the onlooker to see round the object stereoscopically and to shape a solid impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accumulate varied, slight manifestations of inner life in different contexts so the reader perceives depth and weight without direct exposition (example: Milly on the mountain, then among friends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pepper scenes with idle dialogue — use talk only when it contributes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not managed by peppering the surface with animated dialogue by making characters break into talk when they really have nothing to contribute; the end of this is only to cheapen and discredit their talk when it is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure dialogue is motivated and meaningful; avoid inserting talk purely to create action or variety. Dialogue should supply information, reveal character, or enact mental change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the method of dramatization to annex advantages of drama for pictorial subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The less dramatic the subject may be in the strict sense, the more needful to heighten its flat, pictorial, descriptive surface by the arts of drama; the method animates the actual elements of the picture and makes a drama of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with situations that are essentially conditions or states (illness, brooding, internal conflict), use dramatization of small moments and images so the subject 'acts itself' before the reader despite lack of exterior action (examples: The Ambassadors, The Wings of the Dove).
